query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Nanoparticles synthesized with enhanced initial short-range chemical ordering will exhibit greater resistance to phase segregation and oxidation under high-temperature reactive conditions compared to those with random chemical arrangements, due to entropy‐driven stabilization of a uniform solid-solution structure.
generation.material_initial_state: Low noble-metal-content multi-element near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles (e.g., CoNiCuZn-based) with a tunable degree of short-range chemical ordering.
generation.intervention: Control the synthesis process to produce nanoparticles with enhanced, well-defined short-range chemical ordering versus a baseline synthesis producing a random, less ordered chemical distribution.
generation.conditions: Exposure to high-temperature catalytic/thermoelectric environments (773–1173 K) under reactive (e.g., mild oxidizing) atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical ordering acting as a mediator to maintain atomic-scale compositional homogeneity and suppress the nucleation of segregated phases.
generation.mechanism: Entropy-driven stabilization counteracts thermally activated diffusion and elemental segregation. Enhanced short-range order increases the energy barrier for phase separation and oxidation, thereby preserving the single-phase structure over prolonged high-temperature exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with enhanced initial ordering will retain a single-phase solid solution with fewer segregated domains and lower oxidation levels compared to nanoparticles with random chemical ordering under identical reactive high-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized without controlled short-range ordering, which are expected to exhibit higher tendencies for phase separation and oxidation when exposed to high-temperature reactive environments.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable to low noble-metal-content, multi-element nanoparticles synthesized with tunable short-range order and tested within the temperature range of 773–1173 K in reactive environments; results may not directly extrapolate to significantly different compositions, synthesis methods, or broader temperature ranges.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative trend is predicted, the exact quantification of the stabilization effect and the interplay with other degradation mechanisms (e.g., kinetic barriers or surface oxidation) remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of low noble-metal-content multi-element nanoparticles: one set synthesized to have an enhanced initial short-range chemical order and one set with a random chemical arrangement. Expose both sets in a controlled reactive environment at 773–1173 K while performing time-resolved in situ high-temperature TEM and complementary X-ray spectroscopy to monitor morphological changes, phase segregation, and oxidation evolution.
measurements: Real-time imaging of nanoparticle structure (TEM) to detect phase separation or domain formation.
X-ray absorption spectroscopy to monitor oxidation state changes.
Compositional mapping to assess elemental distribution before and after exposure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles with enhanced initial ordering do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in phase segregation or oxidation relative to the baseline (randomly ordered) nanoparticles, then the hypothesis that controlled short-range ordering confers improved stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention in various fields with regard to applications as structural materials, biomaterials, supercapacitors, and catalysts., HEAs comprise mixtures of five or more metallic elements at near equiatomic ratios and form simple single solid-solution phases having lattice structures including face-centered cubic (fcc) and body-centered cubic (bcc)., The high configurational entropy of these alloys stabilizes the solid-solution phase such that this phase appears rather than an intermetallic phase or phase segregation., The severe lattice distortion in these materials that results from differences in the atomic sizes of the constituent elements also causes low atomic diffusivity. The unique synergistic effects resulting from combining multiple elements provide high specific strength, ductility, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, such that HEAs are unique and fascinating materials. High-entropy oxides (HEOs) have aroused growing interest due to fundamental questions relating to their structure formation, phase stability, and the interplay between configurational disorder and physical and chemical properties. Introducing Fe(II) and Mn(II) into a rocksalt HEO is considered challenging, as theoretical analysis suggests that they are unstable in this structure under ambient conditions. Here, we develop a bottom-up method for synthesizing Mn- and Fe-containing rocksalt HEO (FeO-HEO). We present a comprehensive investigation of its crystal structure and the random cation-site occupancy. We show the improved structural robustness of this FeO-HEO and verify the viability of an oxygen sublattice as a buffer layer. Compositional analysis reveals the valence and spin state of the iron species. We further report the antiferromagnetic order of this FeO-HEO below the transition temperature ~218 K and predict the conditions of phase stability of Mn- and Fe-containing HEOs. Our results provide fresh insights into the design and property tailoring of emerging classes of HEOs. Simultaneous in situ X-ray diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy experiments allowed us to study the formation mechanism of noble metal bimetallic and high entropy alloy nanoparticles in depth. The samples were prepared by reduction of single-source precursors. For five-element mixtures, the formation of a single phase occurs more readily than in the binary samples. Under the studied reaction conditions, single-phase formation for binary alloys was restricted to systems where cooperative reduction occurred, while single-phase HEA particles could be obtained even though the elements were reduced consecutively. The findings are explained with a stochastic model that simulates the particle formation process. Regardless of the element interactions, the model quantifies that it is more likely to form a random alloy if more atom types are present in a system with limited free atom mobility. This highlights that knowledge of the formation mechanism is crucial for understanding the material formation pathways. High-entropy and medium-entropy alloys are presumed to have a configurational entropy as high as that of an ideally mixed solid solution (SS) of multiple elements in near-equal proportions. However, enthalpic interactions inevitably render such chemically disordered SSs rare and metastable, except at very high temperatures. Here we highlight the wide variety of local chemical ordering (LCO) that sets these concentrated SSs apart from traditional solvent-solute ones. Using atomistic simulations, we reveal that the LCO of the multi-principal-element NiCoCr SS changes with alloy processing conditions, producing a wide range of generalized planar fault energies. We show that the LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities. This influences the selection of dislocation pathways in slip, faulting, and twinning, and increases the lattice friction to dislocation motion via a nanoscale segment detrapping mechanism. In contrast, severe plastic deformation reduces the LCO towards random SS. Multi-principal-element alloys have been assumed to have the configurational entropy of an ideal solution. Here, we report the computationally aided, entropy-driven design and synthesis of MEA-NPs featuring a uniform alloy structure made up of traditionally immiscible elements. The multi-elemental system has an increased entropy that drives the uniform mixing toward alloy formation, whose compositions were analyzed in a million scale for phase selection. The formation energies of MEA-NPs were predicted using density functional theory (DFT) calculations, and their structures were simulated via a hybrid Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics (MC-MD) approach. Experimentally, we used a rapid and high-temperature method (e.g., 1500 K in 0.5 s) that enables the synthesis of MEA-NPs with an alloy structure that contains fragmented domains and rich interfaces. The synthesized MEA-NPs show excellent thermal stability in terms of both particle size and structure. In addition, we demonstrate the use of these materials for catalytic NH3 decomposition with outstanding performance. We believe that this computationally aided rational design and controllable synthesis method can be generally used to accelerate catalyst discovery in multi-elemental materials.

decision.trend: Early work (PMC6687833) showed that local chemical order in multi-principal alloys alters defect evolution under mechanical stress but offered only indirect clues about high-temperature chemical stability. Subsequent computational approaches (PMC7069714) focused on designing multi-element alloy nanoparticles for catalytic performance at elevated temperatures, highlighting entropy-driven stabilization yet leaving open questions on long-term structural and chemical integrity. More recent investigation of sub-nanometric clusters (PMC10466320) revealed compositional fluctuations and local chemical motifs that transform under redox cycling, suggesting that understanding nanoscale chemical heterogeneity is crucial for predicting stability in real operating environments. While progress has been made in mapping local order and computationally screening compositions, a gap persists in experimentally validating the underlying mechanisms of nanoparticle stability under combined thermal and reactive conditions that mimic catalytic and potential thermoelectric service regimes.
decision.unsolved: Despite computational insights and short-term studies, the key mechanism governing long-term structural and chemical stability of near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles at high temperatures and in reactive environments remains unclear. In particular, the interplay between local chemical ordering, possible topological rearrangements, and partial segregation that could degrade performance or confer resilience has not been conclusively determined.
decision.lever: Conduct time-resolved in situ high-temperature TEM and X-ray spectroscopy on low noble-metal-content multi-element nanoparticles (e.g., CoNiCuZn-based) from 773–1173 K in a controlled reactive environment. Compare samples with carefully varied initial short-range order to isolate changes in local composition, phase formation, and morphological evolution relative to baseline unexposed references. Monitor real-time emergence of segregated domains, shell formation, or stability retention.
decision.why: Building on prior demonstrations of entropy-stabilized alloy design, local chemical ordering, and reversible morphological changes, this approach directly tracks the hypothesized mechanism that entropic stabilization counters high-temperature phase separation in complex compositions. The controlled intervention—tuning the initial short-range chemical ordering—differentiates the entropic-stabilization hypothesis from alternative explanations involving kinetic constraints or surface-driven oxidation. Observing that high-entropy samples resist segregation under reactive conditions (versus reference alloys that degrade) would support the mechanism. This would fail if all samples degrade similarly, falsifying the premise that entropic stabilization is the dominant factor under these operating conditions.
